flashcards.q: Why does a plain conversion-probability model make a bad marketing targeting policy?
flashcards.a: It predicts P(Y=1|X), which is high for both 'sure things' (convert regardless) and 'persuadables' (convert because of treatment) -- it has no signal to tell them apart, so targeting off it wastes spend on sure things and can miss persuadables.

flashcards.q: Define CATE and why it can never be observed for a single individual.
flashcards.a: tau(x) = E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x]. Any unit is either treated or not, so only one of Y(1)/Y(0) is ever observed for it -- the fundamental problem of causal inference. CATE is estimated by comparing groups, never measured directly per-unit.

flashcards.q: Two-model (T-learner) uplift approach and its main weakness?
flashcards.a: Fit mu_1(x) on treated, mu_0(x) on control independently; tau_hat = mu_1-mu_0. Weakness: independently-fit models can have different bias/variance, so subtracting them amplifies noise instead of canceling it, especially with imbalanced arm sizes.

flashcards.q: What does class-transformation uplift modeling require that the two-model approach doesn't?
flashcards.a: Roughly balanced treatment assignment (P(W=1)~=0.5), since Z = Y*W+(1-Y)*(1-W) only maps cleanly to tau(x) = 2P(Z=1|X)-1 under that balance. Unbalanced assignment needs an explicit correction.

flashcards.q: What do causal forests optimize for that standard random forests don't?
flashcards.a: Splits are chosen to maximize heterogeneity in the estimated TREATMENT EFFECT across leaves (not outcome-prediction variance), using 'honest' splitting (disjoint samples for splits vs. effect estimation) to get asymptotically valid confidence intervals on tau(x).

flashcards.q: Difference-in-differences formula and its key untestable assumption?
flashcards.a: DiD = (Y_treat,post - Y_treat,pre) - (Y_control,post - Y_control,pre). Assumption: parallel trends -- absent treatment, both groups would have moved together. Untestable post-hoc; supported only via pre-treatment trend evidence and placebo tests.

flashcards.q: Propensity score matching's identifying assumption, and why has it lost credibility?
flashcards.a: Unconfoundedness/ignorability -- conditional on measured X, treatment is as good as random (no unmeasured confounders), which is unfalsifiable. King & Nielsen (2019) showed matching on a single scalar propensity score can increase covariate imbalance vs. full/exact matching in some regimes.

flashcards.q: What is the exclusion restriction in instrumental variables, and what breaks it?
flashcards.a: The instrument Z must affect the outcome ONLY through its effect on treatment W, and be independent of confounders. It breaks if Z has any other pathway to affect Y -- e.g. an ad-outage instrument also correlating with a site-wide issue that independently affects purchasing.

flashcards.q: When do you use synthetic control instead of plain difference-in-differences?
flashcards.a: When you have one or very few treated units and no single obviously comparable control -- synthetic control builds a data-driven weighted blend of many donor units matching the treated unit's pre-treatment trajectory, rather than relying on one arbitrary control group.

flashcards.q: How do you evaluate an uplift model when you can't observe both potential outcomes per user?
flashcards.a: Qini curve / uplift AUC on a randomized holdout: rank users by predicted uplift, measure cumulative incremental conversions (treated minus control conversion rate) within top-k ranked slices vs random targeting -- classification AUC doesn't work because there's no per-individual uplift ground truth.

flashcards.q: What is a 'sleeping dog' in uplift modeling and why do only uplift models find them?
flashcards.a: A user for whom treatment actively HURTS the outcome (e.g. a retention email that reminds an inattentive customer to cancel). A plain propensity model has no mechanism to detect negative treatment effects; only a model estimating tau(x) directly can surface this quadrant.
